title: Division of Labour and Specialisation
summary: What division of labour and specialisation mean, the types of specialisation, their advantages, disadvantages and limitations.

p: Adam Smith used the example of making pins to show that when a job is split into small tasks and each worker does one task, much more is produced. Division of labour means giving different tasks to different people so that productivity and profit rise.
Example: to build a house, a manager needs masons, plumbers, carpenters, electricians, painters and interior designers. Each uses a special skill and together they finish the building.

Specialisation means that a person, firm or country concentrates on one kind of work or product. There are four types. By process: the work is divided into stages, and each worker or firm does only one stage. By product: a producer makes only one commodity. By sex: some jobs are done only by men or only by women because of custom, tradition or law. Geographical: a region produces one commodity because of its climate and resources (for example cocoa in the south-west of Nigeria and groundnut in the north).
Higher output, large-scale production, saving of time, growth of specialisation, standard goods, and less tiredness.

Greater interdependence: a problem in one stage stops everything. Difficulty in changing jobs (poor mobility). Boredom from repeating the same job. Loss of craftsmanship as workers become machine-minders.
The size of the market, the level of technology, the nature of the good (for example seasonal goods), the supply of inputs such as capital and labour, special talents, and government policy.

title: Economies of Scale and the Scale of Production
summary: Economies and diseconomies of scale (internal and external), advantages and disadvantages of large-scale production, and what limits a firm's growth.

p: Economies of scale are achieved when producing more units costs less per unit. As a firm grows and produces more, its average cost per unit falls. Adam Smith named division of labour and specialisation as two main ways to get this. Diseconomies of scale happen when a firm grows too big and the average cost starts to rise.

Internal economies are cost savings that come from the firm's own growth (for example buying materials in bulk, using machines or splitting management). External economies are savings that all firms in an industry enjoy because the industry has grown or is concentrated in one area, for example a better road network, a skilled labour pool or an industrial estate. Alfred Marshall made this distinction.

Internal diseconomies arise within the firm: poor management, too many workers or technical limits that raise costs. External diseconomies arise outside it: traffic jams, high rents or shortage of workers because many industries crowd into one place.

Internal and external economies; more division of labour; lower cost per unit (one manager can supervise a factory making 1,000 units instead of two managers for two factories of 500); ancillary industries grow up to supply inputs or use by-products, such as around a steel mill.

Danger of over-production and falling prices. Less supervision, so waste and dishonesty. Concentration of wealth in a few hands. Dependence on foreign markets, which can be cut off by war. Individual tastes ignored because goods are uniform.

p: The extent of the market, the availability of capital, the nature of the business, falling price of the product and rising management costs.

title: Economic Systems: Capitalism, Socialism and the Mixed Economy
summary: What an economic system is, and the features, advantages and disadvantages of capitalism, socialism and mixed economies.

p: An economic system is the way a society or government organises and shares its resources, goods and services. It decides how production and consumption are controlled: how things are made, who makes them, how they are shared and who gets access. It is like the set of rules a society follows for money and trade. There are three main types.

In capitalism, individuals own and manage property, and free market forces set prices. Private ownership of the means of production is the main feature; private people decide what to produce, how, and for whom. Examples: the USA, Japan, Australia, Singapore, Switzerland and France (although most governments also play some role).
Features: private ownership, competition, profit motive, accumulation of wealth, free enterprise and individual initiative.
Advantages: customers have choice; efficiency; fast development; hard work is rewarded because people can own property; many forms of production; technology grows; talent is used.
Disadvantages: workers can be exploited; job insecurity and unemployment; unhealthy rivalry; profit at all cost; more crime from the chase for wealth; inequality, since few people control production.

In socialism, the state owns and controls the means of production. Industries are owned by the government, and the aim is the welfare of all citizens. Countries with strong state control have included the former Soviet bloc, Cuba, China (before its reforms) and some African states after independence, such as Tanzania and Mozambique. Most of these have since added market features.
Features: state ownership, welfare focus, no profit motive, full use of resources, prevention of private monopoly and stable prices.
Advantages: fairer sharing of resources, job security, central planning, no private monopoly and no exploitation by private owners.
Disadvantages: little competition; a state monopoly; little creativity; little choice for consumers; laziness because the state provides all.

A mixed economy combines capitalism and socialism. Private property is protected and people have economic freedom, but the government also steps in to meet social aims. Resources are owned jointly by public and private owners. Examples: Britain, Mexico, Peru and, in Africa, Nigeria, Egypt, Kenya and Tanzania.

Features: joint participation and decisions, fair competition, checks and balances, freedom of choice. Advantages: no monopoly, job security, economic development, choice and a mix of the best of both. Disadvantages: corruption and mismanagement, inefficiency, labour exploitation, emphasis on profit at the expense of citizens, and a wide gap between rich and poor.

title: The Basic Economic Problems of Society
summary: The four fundamental questions every society must answer: what, how and for whom to produce, and how efficiently resources are used.

p: Every society has unlimited wants but limited resources. So every society, whether capitalist, socialist or mixed, faces four basic problems.

Because we cannot produce everything, society must decide which goods and services to produce and in what amounts. Factors: cost of production, consumers' income, market demand, availability of resources and consumer needs.

After deciding what to produce, we must choose the method. Factors: the technique of production (labour-intensive or capital-intensive), technological advancement and the relative cost of the factors of production.

Production is not complete until goods reach the final consumers. Factors: the level of consumers' income, the need to satisfy wants, and the economic system. In capitalist and mixed economies, who gets what depends on prices and incomes. In a socialist economy, the state often uses quotas.

Resources are used efficiently if the output is high compared with the inputs. Efficiency depends on the quality of labour (skilled labour raises output and quality) and the techniques of production (machines save time and reduce waste).

title: Firm, Factory, Industry and Business Organisation
summary: The meaning of a firm, a plant (factory) and an industry, the two groups of business organisation, and private and public enterprises.

p: A firm is a business that produces and sells goods or services to earn revenue and profit. A 'company' is any trade or business and includes sole proprietorships, partnerships and corporations, while a firm usually means a business run by two or more partners, such as a law firm.
A plant or factory is the place where a firm produces: the building and equipment in one location (cement plant, textile mill, steel mill).
An industry is a group of firms making similar goods or services for the same market, such as the banking industry, wood industry or insurance industry.

A business organisation is an enterprise set up by an individual, a group or the government to make a profit and/or to provide goods and services. There are two groups: private and public enterprises.

Owned and managed by private individuals, such as a sole proprietorship or a partnership. Characteristics: private people provide the capital; ownership belongs to them; the aim is profit; they are accountable to the owners; and the owners bear the risk.

Owned, controlled and managed by the federal, state or local government. They are often called authorities, corporations, boards or commissions. Examples: the Nigerian Ports Authority (NPA), the Nigerian Television Authority (NTA) and the Nigerian Railway Corporation (NRC). Characteristics: government provides capital; government owns; the aim is social service; managers answer to government; government and taxpayers bear the risk; a board of directors manages.

Private enterprise: owned by individuals; capital from individuals; aim is profit; controlled by owners or their directors; set up by registration; losses are borne by owners. Public enterprise: owned by government; capital from government; aim is social service; controlled by a board appointed by government; set up by an Act; losses are borne by taxpayers.

Problems of private enterprises in Nigeria: inadequate capital, insufficient raw materials, poor management, poor power supply (so firms run generators, which raises cost), and lack of specialisation.

title: Companies and Their Types
summary: What a company is, limited and unlimited liability, private and public limited companies, quoted and unquoted companies.

p: A company is a voluntary group of people who come together to run a business and share the profits. It is a legal body, separate from its owners, formed to reach a common aim.

Limited liability means that owners can lose only the amount they invested. Their private property is safe if the company fails. Unlimited liability means that the owners are fully responsible for all the debts of the business. Sole proprietors and general partners have unlimited liability. The Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA) is the Nigerian law that governs companies.

head: Limited liability
Unlimited liability
rows: Often the same as the owner

p: A private limited company has a small number of shareholders (the old law set a limit of fifty) and may not sell shares to the public. A public limited company (Plc) offers its shares to the general public, and anyone can buy them.

A quoted company has its shares accepted for trading on a stock exchange, which makes it easier to raise capital. Examples in Nigeria: Zenith Bank Plc, Dangote Cement Plc, Cadbury Nigeria Plc and BUA Cement Plc. An unquoted (unlisted) company is not traded on the stock exchange. It may be too small to qualify or have been delisted, and it relies on private investors for capital.

title: Population: Size, Growth and Migration
summary: What population is, birth rate, death rate and migration, population formulas, and the advantages and disadvantages of youthful and ageing populations.

p: Population is the total number of people living in a country or area at a particular time. Three things decide its size and growth: the birth rate, the death rate and migration.

The birth rate (natality rate) is the number of live births per 1,000 people in a year. Birth rate = (number of births ÷ total population) × 1,000. (The notes show × 100, which gives a percentage; for the 'per thousand' form use × 1,000.) Factors: early marriage, desire for a large family, religion, better medical services, higher living standard, ratio of males to females, family planning and infant mortality.

The death rate is the number of deaths per 1,000 people in a year. Death rate = (number of deaths ÷ total population) × 1,000. A high death rate reduces population; a low one raises it. Factors: poor health services, high cost of living, natural disasters, war, ignorance, poverty and high infant mortality.

Migration is the movement of people from one place to another, either for a while or for good. The place people leave is the source region; the place they go to is the receiving region (destination). Immigration is people coming into a country (an immigrant). Emigration is people leaving it (an emigrant). Immigration raises population; emigration lowers it. Factors: disasters, climate, insecurity, economic opportunities, education and wealth, social amenities, political instability and war.
Net migration = immigration − emigration. Natural growth rate = birth rate − death rate. Population growth rate = birth rate − death rate + net migration.

A youthful (increasing) population has a rising share of young people. Advantages: large labour force, large market, respect and attention from other countries, foreign investment and aid. Disadvantages: pressure on resources, crime, shortage of food, crowded cities, and unemployment.

An ageing (declining) population has a rising share of old people. Advantages: lower government spending on children, less crowding, better living standards, more savings and investment. Disadvantages: smaller labour force, under-population, falling GDP, lower rewards for factors, and higher government spending on the elderly.

title: The Labour Market, Labour Force, Efficiency and Mobility of Labour
summary: What the labour market and labour force are, what affects the size of the labour force, what makes labour efficient, and how labour moves between places and jobs.

p: Labour is all human effort, skilled or unskilled, used to produce goods and services. A market is any place or means by which buyers and sellers exchange goods and services at prices set by market forces. The labour market is where buyers of labour (employers) and sellers of labour (workers) meet and agree on wages and conditions.

The labour force (working population) is the total number of people of working age who are able and willing to work. It includes those who have jobs and those looking for jobs, usually between 18 and 65 years, though this differs by country. Factors affecting its size: population (more people, more workers); income (higher incomes attract workers); education (a more educated society has a bigger labour force); home ownership (owning a home reduces mobility); and other local factors.

Efficiency of labour is the productive power of a worker: the ability to do more or better work in a given time. It depends on personal qualities; general education and intelligence; standard of living (good food, clothes, housing); level of technology; state of health; and job security.

Mobility is the ability of workers to move from place to place, job to job or industry to industry. Geographical mobility is movement from one location to another; it is affected by transport cost, government policy, language barriers, family and cultural ties and available infrastructure. Occupational mobility is movement from one job to another; it is affected by the cost and length of training, trade union or professional restrictions, differences in wages, political or religious crises and personal preference.
